questions.question: Explain why a house with a corrugated-iron roof and no ceiling is very hot in summer and cold in winter.
questions.expected_answer: Iron is a good conductor and the roof is thin. In summer, the roof absorbs the Sun's radiation and becomes very hot; heat is conducted straight through and radiates into the room. In winter, warm air rises by convection to the roof and its heat is conducted through the metal to the cold outside. Without a ceiling or insulation, there is nothing to slow these heat flows; gaps also let draughts in and out.

questions.question: Describe four ways of conserving heat energy in a building and explain how each works.
questions.expected_answer: Any four: ceiling with insulation (traps still air, slows conduction and convection through the roof); reflective foil under the roof (reflects radiant heat); thick or cavity walls with thermal mass (slow conduction and store heat by day, release it at night); north-facing windows with an overhang in South Africa (let low winter sun in, block high summer sun); light-coloured roofs (reflect sunlight); sealing gaps with draught strips (stop convection draughts); curtains, double glazing, carpets (add insulation); deciduous trees (shade in summer, sun in winter).

questions.question: Explain three features of a traditional rondavel that make it energy efficient.
questions.expected_answer: Thick thatched roof: many pockets of trapped air make it an excellent insulator, keeping heat out in summer and in during winter. Thick mud or clay walls: poor conductors with high thermal mass, absorbing heat by day and releasing it at night, so inside temperatures stay steady. Round shape: least wall area for the floor space, so less heat is lost, and it resists wind. Also: small windows, mud floors adding thermal mass.
